evidence: obs: agent 28 — EPG parses S/MIME, OpenPGP, DKIM/DMARC, MIP labels; email-triggered file flows bridge EPG and Core
falsifier: No EPG mail-receiving capability is reachable in scope for the hunting environment (out of scope or untestable), or parsing uses strict DER validation with no code-execution-capable deserialization step. Unreachable sink = rejected for this experiment.

title: SAML RelayState open redirect through SimpleSAMLphp SP ACS path
detail: The hunting environment uses SimpleSAMLphp-style SP endpoints (/sp/module.php/saml/... ACS path per agent #14). RelayState is the standard SAML carrier for post-login destination URLs and is attacker-influenced: an SP-initiated login request can carry an arbitrary RelayState value. INPUT: the RelayState parameter on the SP's login/initiate endpoint (and on the SAMLRequest redirect binding). HOW it would be tested (later, under authorization): initiate the SSO flow with RelayState set to a canary external URL and observe where the session lands after authentication completes (or after the IdP interaction, using consenting test accounts). CONFIRMING BEHAVIOR: after successful authentication the browser lands on the attacker-supplied external URL, proving the SP redirects to an unvalidated RelayState. CHAIN POTENTIAL: an unvalidated RelayState is the classic SSO phishing enabler and can also chain with the MCP Server OAuth localhost:9999 callback model (9.5+) if authorization-code flows pass through the same redirect handling. CONFIRMATION requires the external landing to be reproducible and attributable to RelayState (not to an IdP-configured default landing).
evidence: Agent #14: 'SAML 2.0 SSO (SimpleSAMLphp-style /sp/module.php/saml/... ACS path; IdPs incl. Entra ID/ADFS, Ping Identity)'; world model open question #5 asks where the LDAP/SSO integration points are — this is that integration point. SimpleSAMLphp historically redirects to RelayState without strict validation when not configured with a return-URL allowlist; untested on this target.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) the SP rejects non-whitelisted RelayState values (error page or forced default landing) for an external canary across repeated trials; or (b) RelayState is verified against a signed request or session-bound target before redirect; or (c) the hunting environment has no SSO login path enabled (local-auth only), making RelayState unreachable.

title: Login ?next=/?returnUrl= parameter honored as absolute external URL after authentication
detail: Enterprise login pages commonly accept a post-login destination (?next=, ?returnUrl=, ?redirect=, ?return_to=) so a session-timeout bounce can return the user to the protected page. INPUT: the destination query parameter on the Core login page (and on the session-timeout redirect to /login). HOW it would be tested (later, under authorization): request the login page with the parameter set to a canary external URL, then complete a login with a consenting test account and observe the final 302/location target. CONFIRMING BEHAVIOR: post-login the browser receives a 302 to (or renders through) the exact attacker-supplied external URL, with the session still attached — i.e., the parameter is copied into the redirect without host allowlisting. CHAIN POTENTIAL: combined with any session-identifier-in-URL feature (e.g., share-link tokens, email-gateway one-time links) a redirect can carry bearer tokens to an external host in the Referer/Location; it is also the standard phishing landing that inherits the program's real trust domain. CONFIRMATION requires the external 302 to be reproducible across sessions and not a one-off error path.
evidence: World model: SPA shell at / references /login_config (auth configuration surface, full body fetch hangs — needs browser-rendered fetch by an eligible agent); agent #49 (reflected-xss) independently hypothesized redirect params (?next=/?returnUrl=/?redirect=) exist on auth pages. Untested on this target.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) the parameter is validated to relative paths only (external canary is replaced by a default landing page, consistently, across trials); or (b) no destination parameter exists on the login flow (post-login always lands on a fixed dashboard); or (c) the value is reflected only in-page with proper encoding and never used as a redirect target (302 Location never contains the external host).

title: Logout/SLO redirect parameter (logout?redirect= / SAML single-logout ReturnTo) issued as unvalidated 302
detail: Logout endpoints and SAML single-logout flows frequently accept a post-logout landing (?redirect=, ?returnTo=, ?next=, or SAML LogoutResponse Destination) so the IdP/SP can return the user to a branded page. INPUT: the post-logout destination parameter on the Core logout URL and on any SAML SLO endpoint. HOW it would be tested (later, under authorization): issue an authenticated logout with the parameter set to a canary external URL and inspect the 302 Location chain. CONFIRMING BEHAVIOR: the server answers with a 302 to the exact external canary URL, proving the logout redirect is unvalidated. CHAIN POTENTIAL: this is the lowest-value redirect alone, but it matters as a redirector gadget — a logout URL under the trusted kiteworks domain that bounces to arbitrary external hosts is a standard payload-delivery primitive in phishing chains, and it can be combined with the RelayState vector (H1) for multi-hop chains that inherit the program's domain trust. CONFIRMATION requires the external 302 to be the documented response to the parameter, reproducible, and not issued by an intermediary (proxy/CDN).
evidence: World model: SSO/SAML integrations (Entra ID/ADFS, Ping Identity) per agent #14, which implies SLO/logout endpoints exist; 'Auto Redirect IP or Range forcing SSO by source IP' (obs_app n28) shows the platform already implements redirect-on-condition logic. Untested on this target.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) logout ignores the parameter (always lands on a fixed page) or validates it to relative/same-origin paths; or (b) the SAML SLO flow requires a signed request carrying the return URL, so no attacker-settable parameter exists; or (c) no logout/SLO endpoint is reachable in the hunting environment.

title: Zip-slip in server-side archive extraction (uploaded archives)
detail: Kiteworks MFT handles file transfer flows that ingest archives; archive previews and automation workflows extract ZIP entries server-side. INPUT: archive entry names (the most likely path-flavored attacker input) inside an archive uploaded through a legitimate file flow. Confirming behavior (future authorized test with synthetic data only): an entry name containing '../' or an absolute path materializes outside the extraction root (write primitive). Falsifier: extraction rejects or canonicalizes entries (all entries land inside the extraction root), which disproves the weakness.
evidence: Class prior: zip-slip is a durable MFT/extraction bug class; world model notes Apache Airflow lineage in MFT history (automation unpack flows). No archive endpoints mapped yet; passive GET of /robots.txt returned empty, /.well-known/security.txt timed out (no endpoint evidence either way).
falsifier: Disproven if every entry of a test archive extracts strictly within the extraction root (traversal sequences rejected, flattened, or canonicalized before write).

title: Path traversal in download/preview endpoint via filename or path parameter
detail: Secure file-sharing apps expose download and preview URLs; where the server resolves a user-influenced filename/path parameter to a filesystem path without canonicalization, '../' sequences escape the intended directory. INPUT: the filename or path query/body parameter on a download or preview endpoint (not the share-link token, to avoid the program-excluded 'anyone after authentication' authorization class). Confirming behavior: a traversal payload returns content from outside the intended directory tree. Falsifier: the endpoint resolves opaque IDs/tokens rather than paths, or canonicalizes and enforces a prefix check, yielding identical 4xx responses for traversal vs garbage input.
evidence: World model open question 3 (upload/share flow mapping in progress); no download endpoints mapped yet. Class prior: preview generators and download handlers are classic traversal sites in file platforms.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) download/preview URLs carry only opaque tokens/IDs with no path parameter; or (b) traversal and random-garbage inputs return identical error responses with no content differential across repeated trials.

title: Traversal via unsanitized original filename in bulk-download/export archive generation
detail: Kiteworks MFT supports bulk download/export flows that generate a ZIP server-side from user-selected files; if the server builds archive entry names from user-controlled original filenames, a filename containing '../' or '/' poisons the generated archive (self-inflicted archive poisoning: server later re-extracting or a recipient extracting writes outside the target dir). INPUT: the original filename supplied at upload time, later consumed by the export/archive-generation flow. Confirming behavior: the generated archive preserves traversal-bearing entry names verbatim. Falsifier: filenames are sanitized (slashes/dots stripped or replaced) before upload persistence, or archive entry names are generated from opaque IDs so the original filename never reaches the archive.
evidence: Class prior: export-as-ZIP flows in sharing platforms historically preserve raw filenames; world model confirms MFT is in scope with undetected stack. No upload or export endpoints mapped yet.
falsifier: Disproven if uploaded filenames with path separators are visibly normalized on upload (renamed/sanitized in the UI or API response), or if generated archives use opaque entry names rather than original filenames.

title: Traversal in preview/thumbnail cache write path derived from document path or name
detail: Document preview pipelines render files to a cache directory; where the cache filename is derived from a user-influenced document path or display name without canonicalization, '../' in the name can direct the cache write outside the cache root (write primitive) or cause cache-key collisions serving another file's preview. INPUT: document name or folder path feeding the preview renderer. Confirming behavior: a traversal-bearing document name produces a cache artifact outside the expected cache directory, or previews of distinct documents collide/swap. Falsifier: cache keys are content hashes or opaque IDs with no path derivation, or name-based keys are canonicalized and prefix-checked before write.
evidence: Class prior: preview/thumbnail caches are a recurring traversal site in file platforms; Kiteworks Core centers on file sharing with previews (open question 3). No preview endpoints mapped yet; passive surface check (robots.txt empty, security.txt timeout) gave no endpoint evidence.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) preview artifacts are keyed by opaque content hash or document ID; or (b) traversal-bearing names yield preview outputs identical in placement to sanitized names, with no file materializing outside the cache root.

title: BOLA-1: Comment endpoints bypass parent-file permission checks
detail: GET /rest/comments/{id}, PUT /rest/comments/{id}, DELETE /rest/comments/{id} operate directly on the comment ID. The API has file-scoped comment listing (GET /rest/files/{id}/comments) that implies permission is checked at the file level, but the bare /rest/comments/{id} endpoints may validate only authentication + that the comment exists, not that the caller has access to the parent file/folder. A comment ID harvested from a shared file could be read, edited, or deleted by a user with no access to that file.
evidence: API v28 client docs list restCommentsIdGet/Put/Delete on GET/PUT/DELETE /rest/comments/{id} as standalone operations; separate file-scoped listing exists at /rest/files/{id}/comments. No docs statement found tying {id}-level comment ops to parent-file ACL checks.
falsifier: Authenticated low-priv user requests GET /rest/comments/{comment_id} for a comment on a file they cannot access and receives 403/404 (or 200 only when the caller has access to the parent file).

title: BOLA-2: File member role update reachable by non-owner members
detail: PUT /rest/files/{id}/members/{member_user_id} (Update members in the file) and DELETE /rest/files/{id}/members/{member_user_id} (Delete member from the file) may enforce only that the caller is a member of the file, not that the caller holds owner/manage permission. If so, a read-only file member can elevate their own role to editor, or remove other members / the owner.
evidence: API v28 client docs list restFilesIdMembersMemberUserIdPut/Delete on PUT/DELETE /rest/files/{id}/members/{member_user_id}. Folder-level members endpoint POST /rest/folders/{id}/members (Add multiple members) exists as a separate bulk op. Docs do not state an owner-only requirement on the per-member update.
falsifier: A non-owner (viewer/editor) file member attempts PUT /rest/files/{id}/members/{other_user_id} to change a role, or their own role to editor, and the server returns 403 for every such attempt while owners succeed.

title: BOLA-3: Version promote action lacks per-object write check
detail: POST /rest/files/{id}/versions/{version_id}/actions/promote (promote specified file version) is a state-changing action on a version object nested under a file. It may check authentication and file existence but not the caller's write permission on the file, letting a read-only viewer rewrite file history (rollback attacks, content substitution behind a share link).
evidence: API v28 client docs list restFilesIdVersionsVersionIdActionsPromotePost on POST /rest/files/{id}/versions/{version_id}/actions/promote. Versioning endpoints include per-version content download (GET .../versions/{version_id}/content), so version objects are directly addressable by ID.
falsifier: A viewer-role member of the file (read-only, no write) attempts the promote action and receives 403, while an editor-role member succeeds.

title: BOLA-4: File content download keyed only on unauthenticated ID lookup
detail: GET /rest/files/{id}/content (Download a file) and GET /rest/files/{id} (Retrieve information about the file specified) take a bare file ID. If the ID-space is predictable/guessable and the authorization check is a single ACL lookup that fails open on shared-folder membership edges (e.g., caller has access to a PARENT folder but not the file, or was removed as member), a cross-user IDOR leaks metadata or bytes.
evidence: API v28 client docs list restFilesIdContentGet (GET /rest/files/{id}/content) and restFilesIdGet (GET /rest/files/{id}). Program excludes 'anyone after authentication' file disclosure as an accepted-risk class, which signals the area is sensitive — hypothesis targets only access OUTSIDE the documented sharing model, not the excluded class.
falsifier: Requesting content/metadata for a file ID owned by another user (no shared relationship) returns 403/404 consistently, including for IDs adjacent in the ID space and for files whose parent folder was previously shared.

title: XXE via SAML IdP metadata XML import in admin authentication settings
detail: Entry point: admin console SSO/SAML configuration where the administrator imports or pastes the identity provider's metadata XML (standard Kiteworks admin flow for SAML 2.0 IdP integration). If the metadata XML is parsed server-side with a Java/.NET XML parser that resolves external DTD/entities (default-insecure DocumentBuilderFactory / XmlDocument settings), a crafted metadata file containing a DOCTYPE with an external entity could trigger XXE during import/validation. Confirming behavior: import response or validation error reflects resolved entity content, or an out-of-band request is issued to a collaborator URL embedded in the entity (blind XXE). Kiteworks product docs list SAML 2.0 IdP integration as a standard supported feature.
evidence: Public Kiteworks API/admin documentation describes SAML_2.0 as a supported authorization/authentication type (legacy Accellion admin guide mirrored at watoniworawi.weebly.com admin guide; Kiteworks data-form-security whitepaper lists 'OAuth 2.0 and SAML integration with enterprise identity providers'). Hunting-environment target unreachable from sandbox (curl timeout, browser.open no content), so no live confirmation of the admin SSO UI on the bounty host; passive grade only.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) IdP metadata is only consumed via copy-paste fields (entity ID, cert, endpoints) with no XML document parsing; (b) the metadata parser rejects DOCTYPE / disables external entities (disallow-doctype-decl or equivalent), so a benign probe DOCTYPE is rejected or ignored; or (c) metadata import is not exposed in the hunting environment.

title: XXE via Secure Data Forms / Web Forms definition import (XML templates)
detail: Entry point: Secure Data Forms (formerly Secure Web Forms) module lets admins design structured forms; if form definitions can be imported/exported as XML (common for form-builder products), the import endpoint parses administrator-supplied XML. A DOCTYPE with external entities in the form-definition XML could be resolved during import. Confirming behavior: entity content appears in the imported form's preview/fields, or a validation error echoes resolved content. Note: this is speculative on the format - Kiteworks docs describe web form design via admin guide/training video but do not publicly confirm an XML import path, so format must be verified first.
evidence: Kiteworks Statement of Work and best-practices docs describe Secure Web Forms as admin-designed predefined forms collecting structured data. No public doc found confirming XML-based form import; hunting host unreachable, so this rests on product-module existence only.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) form definitions are created only through the UI wizard and stored/transferred as JSON with no XML parsing; or (b) the import endpoint, if any, accepts only schema-validated XML with DOCTYPE rejected.

title: XXE via AS4/ebMS SOAP envelope parsing in MFT B2B transfer gateway
detail: Entry point: Kiteworks Managed File Transfer module handles B2B file exchange; enterprise MFT products commonly expose AS2/AS4 receive endpoints that parse SOAP/XML messaging envelopes (ebMS 3.0/AS4 uses SOAP with attachments). If the hunting environment exposes an AS4/SOAP receive endpoint, the eb:Messaging header/body XML could be parsed with external-entity resolution enabled. Confirming behavior: an external entity inside the SOAP body is resolved (reflected in the MDN/error or an outbound request), producing file disclosure or SSRF. Kiteworks public docs emphasize MFT as a core product; AS4/SOAP exposure on the bounty host is unverified.
evidence: Kiteworks MFT is a scoped product per the YesWeHack program page; AS4/SOAP endpoint existence is NOT publicly confirmed for Kiteworks (inference from MFT product category only). Hunting host unreachable; zero endpoint evidence.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) no SOAP/AS2/AS4 receive endpoint is exposed on the hunting environment; or (b) any such endpoint rejects DOCTYPE or uses a hardened parser (no external entity resolution observed on probe).

title: XXE in document preview/conversion pipeline via OOXML or PDF/XFA uploads
detail: Entry point: Kiteworks secure file sharing includes document preview/thumbnail generation; preview pipelines often shell out to converters (e.g., LibreOffice, Apache Tika-style text extraction). A crafted .docx (document.xml with external entities - rarely resolved by ZIP-based parsers, so lower value) or a PDF containing an XFA form (XFA is XML and has a documented 2025/2026 XXE history: CVE-2025-54988 / CVE-2025-66516 in Apache Tika XFA handling, disclosed via crafted PDFs) processed by the preview/extraction chain could trigger XXE. Confirming behavior: extracted/preview text contains resolved external-entity content, or an outbound request fires during processing. This is the highest-severity shape (authenticated-user upload -> server-side parse) but depends entirely on the converter stack, which is unmapped.
evidence: Preview/thumbnail conversion is standard in file-sharing products; the Tika XFA XXE (CVE-2025-54988, PoC published ~Sep 2026 per GitHub kmkz/exploits) demonstrates this exact class is live in 2026-era stacks. No evidence the Kiteworks hunting env uses a vulnerable converter; converter stack is unmapped on the bounty host.
falsifier: Disproven if: (a) the hunting environment performs no server-side document text extraction/preview (client-side rendering only); or (b) the converter chain is identified and rejects or sandboxes XFA/embedded-XML processing (e.g., XFA disabled in the parser config).

title: desanitize() decode-then-render: stored DOM-XSS via tenant config values
detail: /login_config defines desanitize(str) which HTML-entity-decodes server-injected config values ('->', &->&, "->", <-><, >->>) and strips ALL backslashes, applied to vue_config fields (serviceName, labels, disclaimer, ipBlockMsg, link.getStarted, link.contactUs, info.contactUs). If the Vue SPA renders any of these fields through an HTML sink (v-html/dangerouslySetInnerHTML/innerHTML) in the 21 unfetched chunks, a tenant/admin-set value stored HTML-encoded at rest is decoded back to raw markup client-side before injection = stored DOM-XSS affecting all tenant visitors. Not self-XSS (victim is other users of the tenant).
evidence: GET /login_config (200, 1190 bytes, 2026-09-27): full desanitize() source captured; signin.f7b86212.js chunk (49KB) contains zero innerHTML/document.write/eval sinks, so sink must be confirmed in remaining ~21 chunks. CSP is script-src 'self', which would block inline script execution but not necessarily non-script HTML injection impact.
falsifier: Grep the remaining /static/js/*.js chunks for innerHTML|v-html|dangerouslySetInnerHTML consuming vue_config/*config* fields; if all rendering is textContent/React-escaped with no HTML sink reachable from config values, reject.

title: Tenant-configurable link URLs rendered as anchor href with target=_new (javascript: URL)
detail: vue_config.link.getStarted, link.contactUs, info.contactUs are rendered as links with target=_new per code comment ('this part describe values used for links - a href target new'). Empty in this environment but tenant-configurable. If the app sets the href from config without scheme allow-listing, a tenant admin (or a tenant-config injection flaw) setting javascript:alert(document.domain) yields stored XSS executed in the victim's session on the login page. Source=tenant config, sink=anchor href assignment/navigation.
evidence: /login_config source: link:{getStarted:'',contactUs:''}, info:{contactUs:''} plus comment 'used for links - a href target new'. No scheme validation visible in /login_config or signin.f7b86212.js.
falsifier: Inspect link-rendering code in remaining chunks for href scheme validation (http/https allow-list) or confirm these config fields are not tenant-editable; if either holds, reject.

title: location.search query params flow into window.location.assign via x.fI URL builder
detail: In signin chunk: query params parsed from window.location.search by x.JO, merged into a URL by x.fI, then window.location.assign() executes it.
